crossReferences.why: The same formulation, given as the reply when they demand to know when the promise will arrive.
Places the identical principle beside the statement that no town was destroyed without a known decree.
Applies the same rule to the individual soul rather than the community, with the same finality.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been treating as permanent because it has lasted a long time: a job, a neighbourhood, an arrangement in your family. Say to yourself, plainly, that it has an end date you do not know. Then do one small thing you would do if you knew it was closer than you think. One thing, today, not a plan.

studies.title: Messengers From Among You
studies.meaning: The condition attached to the messengers is easy to read past. They come from among you, which rules out the arrival of a being of another order and makes recognition possible and refusal harder. Their work is described with a verb meaning to follow a track. Then the response that secures the outcome is given as two things, not one: guarding oneself, and putting right. The second is active and outward. What follows is the Quran's recurring formula about fear and grief, in its conditional rather than its declarative form.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to the whole human line rather than to one audience, which is why it is phrased as a standing condition rather than an event. The Quraysh had objected that a messenger should be an angel or at least a man of greater means, and the wording answers that objection without arguing with it. No occasion of revelation is reported. The surah is about to give six such messengers in sequence, all of them local men.

keyTerms.note: From the root for following footprints. The messengers are described as tracking the signs rather than composing a message, which puts them in the position of guides reading ground already marked.
The root means to place a shield between yourself and harm. It describes protective care rather than dread, so the usual translation as fear catches only the reason for the action, not the action.
A verb for mending what is broken, used of reconciling parties and of restoring land to use. Paired with self-protection, it turns an inward posture into work done on something outside oneself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger in Arabia was a known figure with a defined role. Tribes sent men to carry terms, and the messenger's standing came from being one of the people he spoke for, since a stranger could not be trusted to deliver a message faithfully or to be held to account for it afterwards. To say the messengers would be from among you was to describe the only arrangement the audience already considered credible.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic here uses an emphatic conditional construction that combines two particles and adds a heavy verb ending, a form the Quran reserves for situations presented as certain to occur rather than merely possible. The English if or when cannot carry it. The grammar effectively says: when they do come, and they will.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is defined by ordinariness rather than by spectacle. A messenger is one of the people he addresses, which makes his life part of the message and removes the excuse that the standard was set by a different kind of creature. And the security promised is attached to a pair, guarding and mending, so an inward orientation is not accepted on its own. What settles the matter is whether anything was repaired.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same condition to jinn and humans together, messengers from among you relating My signs.
Records the objection this wording answers, that people refused to accept a human being as messenger.
Gives the same promise about fear and grief at the moment of the descent to earth.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing in your immediate reach that is broken and could be mended by you this week: a rift with a cousin, a promise you let lapse, a mess in a shared space that everyone steps around. Fix that one. The passage pairs inward care with outward repair, and only one of the two leaves evidence.

studies.title: Too Proud To Accept
studies.meaning: Two things are named and they are not the same. The first is calling the signs false, a judgement about content. The second is being too great for them, a posture that has nothing to do with evidence. The Arabic construction of the second verb implies turning away from something as beneath you. Placing them together suggests the classical reading that the verdict often follows the posture rather than producing it: a person decides they are above receiving instruction, and the arguments arrive afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The leading families of Quraysh objected repeatedly that the message had come to a man of no particular standing and that its early followers were poor men and slaves, an objection about rank rather than about content. This ayah sits directly after the promise made to those who guard themselves and put right, giving the alternative in the same breath. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form, so it means to pronounce something a lie rather than merely to doubt it. The Quran uses it far more often than the word for disbelief, because it names an act of judgement made aloud.
The same root as the refusal earlier in this surah, in a form meaning to seek greatness for oneself. Followed by the preposition used here, it means turning away from a thing as unworthy.
The ordinary word for the people you keep company with and belong among. Applying it to the Fire describes belonging rather than sentence, which is a quieter and stranger idea than imprisonment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society was arranged by precedence, and precedence was performed daily. Who spoke first in the assembly, who was seated where at a feast, whose guarantee a stranger needed. A man of the leading clans could not be seen taking instruction from someone below him without the whole city noticing. The cost of accepting the message was therefore social before it was anything else, and it was paid in public.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs used here for denial and self-magnifying recur as a pair throughout the Quran, appearing together in this exact combination in several surahs. Classical commentators observe that the Book almost never presents rejection as a purely intellectual failure. Wherever the refusal is described at length, something about standing or pride is named alongside the argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is located partly in the will rather than entirely in the intellect. The passage does not say the deniers lacked evidence; it says they were too great for what they were given, which makes receptivity a moral condition. That is an uncomfortable claim, since it means a person can be perfectly capable of following an argument and still unable to accept it, and it explains why the Quran so often appeals to humility before it appeals to proof.

crossReferences.why: The first refusal in the surah, made on exactly these grounds and answered with expulsion.
Says God seals the heart of every arrogant tyrant who disputes the signs without warrant given.
Describes one who hears the signs recited, persists in arrogance as if unhearing, and mocks them.

studies.applyIt: Notice today whether there is anyone whose correction you would find it hard to accept, not because they are wrong but because of who they are. A younger colleague, a sibling, someone whose life you privately consider less successful than yours. Let one such correction land this week without adjusting for the source. That is the whole exercise.

studies.title: Where Are They Now
studies.meaning: A question is asked that expects no answer, pairing invention against God with denying His signs as the extreme of wrongdoing. Then a phrase commentators read in two ways: their share of the Book reaches them, meaning either what was decreed for them of lifespan and provision, or their portion as recorded. Both readings agree the point is that nothing is cut short. The scene that follows is the moment of death, and the envoys ask one question. The answer, when it comes, is a confession nobody demanded.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who maintained intermediaries at the sanctuary and expected them to intercede. Their objection to the message was not that God did not exist but that these figures had standing with Him. This ayah does not argue the point. It moves the question to the one moment when the arrangement will be tested, and lets the answer be given by the people who made it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for cutting leather to a pattern before stitching it. A fabrication in Arabic is something cut and assembled to fit, which describes invented religion more precisely than the word lie does.
From the root for paying a debt completely. Death is described as a collection of what is owed in its entirety, with nothing left outstanding, rather than as a seizure or an ending.
The verb for losing one's way, here with the objects doing the straying. What was relied on is described as having wandered off, which is a deliberately undignified word for a failed patron.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the security system of Arabia. A man without a strong protector had no recourse if he was robbed or killed, and the arrangement was renewed publicly so everyone knew who stood behind whom. Failing to appear when your client called was the worst thing a patron could do to his own name. The scene here uses that vocabulary exactly: the protectors are summoned at the one moment they are needed, and they are simply absent.
studies.didYouKnow: The testimony at the end is given by the people themselves, against themselves, and no accusation precedes it. This pattern recurs across the Quran's death and judgement scenes: witnesses are called, records are opened, limbs speak, but the decisive statement is often the person's own. Classical commentators note that the Book almost never needs to convict anyone who has not first agreed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the falseness of an arrangement not in an argument against it but in the moment it is required to work. Whatever a person leans on will either bear weight at that point or will not, and the Quran is content to let that be the test. It also insists that nothing owed is withheld in the meantime: the lifespan runs its course, the provision arrives, and the reckoning waits, which is a description of patience on God's part rather than of indifference.

crossReferences.why: The same scene of arriving alone, with the intercessors relied on described as cut away and lost.
Repeats the question directly, where are your partners now, and receives the same admission of absence.
Shows what was invented straying from them at the reckoning, using the identical verb for going astray.

studies.applyIt: Name, honestly, the thing you assume will hold you up if everything else fails. Savings, a qualification, a particular person, your own competence. Do not disparage it; most of these are real supports. Just ask whether you have quietly promoted it from a help to a guarantee. That distinction is the whole subject of this passage, and it is worth ten minutes.

studies.title: Each Curses Its Sister
studies.meaning: The instruction is to enter among communities that went before, jinn and human together, which places the newcomers in a lineage rather than in a category. Then the behaviour: each group entering curses the one before it. When all have arrived, the last address the first and ask for their punishment to be doubled, naming them as the cause. The reply grants the doubling and extends it to everyone, and closes with a clause that refuses to explain: but you do not know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a society organised entirely around following. A man's religion, trade, alliances and enemies came with his clan, and the defence that one had simply done what one's people did was the most natural thing a person could say. The surah has already recorded that defence in the mouths of those who appealed to their fathers. Here it is heard again, at the point where it is tested.

keyTerms.note: Communities are given a kinship word, since the noun for a community is grammatically feminine. Calling the earlier group a sister makes the cursing a family quarrel, which sharpens rather than softens the scene.

A verb for successive groups overtaking one another until all are gathered. It carries the sense of a crowd arriving in waves, each catching the one ahead, rather than of a single assembly convened at once.
The word means a fold or a doubling and can indicate more than twice over. The same root gives the Quran's word for multiplied reward, so the vocabulary of increase runs in both directions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society had no individuals in the modern sense. You were of a clan, and the clan answered for you: it paid your blood money, avenged your death, and bore your disgrace. Turning on your own people was close to unthinkable, and the poets treat it as the last collapse. A scene in which each generation curses the one that raised it would have struck the first listeners as a description of the end of the world.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply to the request for a double punishment does not deny it, adjust it, or defend the leaders. It grants the doubling and extends it to the petitioners themselves, then closes with a clause telling them they do not know. Classical commentators note that the Quran often answers a question in judgement scenes by widening it rather than by explaining it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Following is not accepted as a transfer of responsibility. Both parties carry a double weight, the one for leading and the one for choosing to be led, and the passage refuses to let the second be reduced to a misfortune. The mutual cursing makes a further point. What bound these groups together was never solidarity in the first place, since it dissolves the moment there is nothing left to gain from it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same complaint, we obeyed our chiefs and they misled us, with the same request for doubling.
Shows the leaders answering that they had no power over the followers, who chose to respond.
States that close friends will be enemies to each other on that Day, except those who guarded themselves.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you do mainly because the people around you do it, and that you would not choose on your own. It does not have to be wrong. Just identify it accurately and say why you do it, without the usual softening. Owning a borrowed decision as yours is not the same as changing it, and it is the part that is actually available today.

studies.title: No Advantage Over Us
studies.meaning: The reply completes an exchange begun in the preceding ayah. The followers had asked for their leaders to receive double; the leaders now answer that the followers hold no advantage over them. Commentators read the word for advantage in its ordinary sense of surplus or superiority, so the argument is that nobody's position was better and nobody was compelled. Then the closing clause supplies the standard being applied. Not who led whom, but what each one earned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a passage constructed as a courtroom scene with the parties speaking in turn. The audience lived under a system where a clan chief answered for his people and their conduct was credited or debited to him. This exchange takes that arrangement apart in two sentences and does so from the chief's side, letting the leaders be the ones who deny that anybody was carried.

keyTerms.note: The root means what is left over, and the same word elsewhere in the Quran means God's bounty. Here it is used for social advantage, so the two senses sit one root apart.

A verb from eating and hospitality, used across the Quran for punishment arriving. Tasting is direct and personal knowledge, which is why the word replaces any expression meaning to suffer or undergo.
The everyday word for acquiring by work or trade, used of wages and profit. It makes each person's record an account they built themselves rather than a verdict handed to them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Responsibility in Arabia was collective by design. If a man killed, his kin paid; if a clan gave protection, every member was bound by it. This is what made a chief's word worth following, and it is also why the followers in this scene expect the arrangement to hold. The reply describes a place where the accounts are separated out, which for that audience was the strangest part of the picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The exchange is arranged with unusual symmetry. The later group speaks first, blaming the earlier; the earlier group answers; and the divine reply has already come between the two, granting the doubling to everybody. Classical commentators note that the Quran lets both parties make their case in full before the verdict, and that neither one's argument is refuted, only widened.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Accountability is presented as individual without denying that influence is real. The leaders are not exonerated, since the divine reply has already assigned them a double portion; what is refused is the follower's claim to be a bystander in his own life. That leaves both facts standing at once, which is harder than either the view that people are simply products of their circumstances or the view that circumstances do not count.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same dispute at greater length, with the weak and the arrogant each answering the other.
States the principle behind this scene: no bearer carries another's load, and each has what he strove for.
Applies the same rule across generations: that community has passed, theirs is what they earned.

studies.applyIt: Think of a habit you picked up from someone you looked up to and still half attribute to them. Try describing it once today in the first person, with no mention of where it came from. It is your habit now, whoever handed it over. The sentence is uncomfortable to say and it is accurate, which is the point.

studies.title: Until The Camel Passes
studies.meaning: Two things are refused, and the pair matters: the gates of the sky will not open, and they will not enter the Garden. Commentators connect the first to the rising of deeds and souls, so the closure works in both directions. Then the impossible condition, which reads as flatly in Arabic as it does in English. Some classical authorities record a second reading of the word for camel that would make it a thick twisted rope, better suited to a needle, and the tradition preserves both without settling it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to men whose refusal of the message was bound up with their standing in the city. The image draws on things the audience handled daily, since Mecca ran on camels and every household had a needle. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage sits between two judgement scenes and states the outcome plainly before the surah returns to the dialogue between the two groups.

keyTerms.note: The first word means a small aperture, the same one behind the word for poison, which enters through the smallest opening. It names the hole precisely rather than the needle in general.
From the root for spreading something flat and soft, used elsewhere in the Quran of the earth prepared as a cradle. Applying the word of comfort to this place is the whole force of the line.
A plural for things that cover something over, from a verb for enveloping. Paired with the bedding beneath, the two words assemble a made bed, which is a colder image than flames would be.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The camel was the largest thing in Arabian life and the measure of everything valuable: bride price, blood money, a family's whole estate. The needle was among the smallest possessions anyone owned, carried by every woman who repaired a tent or a garment. Putting the two together was not an exotic figure of speech. It set the biggest and the smallest objects in the audience's world side by side.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered as bedding here is used elsewhere in the Quran for the earth itself, spread out as a cradle for human beings. The same noun does duty for the ground under a sleeping child and for what is described in this ayah, and the reversal is entirely carried by the vocabulary rather than stated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names arrogance twice, once in the description of the offence and once in the closing formula about wrongdoers, which places the whole scene under a heading that has nothing to do with intellectual error. It also handles impossibility carefully. Rather than announcing that entry is barred, it states a condition and lets the condition be absurd, which is a way of saying the door is not locked so much as it is a door nothing of that shape fits through.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a spread bed of the earth itself, made ready for people to live on.
Describes good words and righteous deeds ascending, which is what the closed gates of the sky imply.
Repeats the charge of arrogance towards the signs and asks whether Hell is not the abode of the proud.

studies.applyIt: Pick the smallest opening in your day, the one place where something good could get through if you let it: two minutes before you sleep, the walk from the car to the door. Put one thing in it. Not a programme, one thing, the same one for a week. The passage is about apertures, and small ones are the only kind most of us actually have.

studies.title: Never Beyond Its Capacity
studies.meaning: A clause interrupts the sentence. The ayah is describing those who believe and do sound works, and before it reaches its conclusion it stops to say that no soul is charged beyond what it can hold. Commentators read the interruption as deliberate, placed exactly where a listener would start measuring themselves against the standard just named and finding themselves short. Only then does the sentence finish. The interruption is not an exemption from the requirement; it is a statement about how the requirement was set.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a run of ayat alternating between the two outcomes. The early community in Mecca included slaves, the poor and people with very little freedom of action, for whom a demand for sound works could have read as a demand for resources they did not have. No occasion of revelation is reported. The parenthesis addresses that difficulty directly without altering the description around it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to burden with something costly or troublesome. The verb assumes the task is difficult, so the clause does not deny hardship; it sets a ceiling on it.
From the root for breadth and room. The word names how much space a thing has rather than how strong it is, so the measure is individual and can differ from one person to the next.
From a root meaning to be fit or in good order, and used of mending what is damaged. Righteous deeds in this vocabulary are things that work rather than things that impress.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Loads were assessed constantly in a caravan economy. A camel was packed to a known limit, and a driver who overloaded an animal lost it on the road, so the whole trade depended on honest estimates of what each beast could carry across a given distance. The vocabulary of imposing a burden and of capacity was technical and familiar, and it was understood that the limit varied from one animal to another.
studies.didYouKnow: This clause appears three times in the Quran with almost identical wording, and one of those is the closing supplication of the longest surah, where the community asks not to be charged with what it cannot bear. Here the same sentence is not a request but a statement, placed inside a description rather than at the end of a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The relationship between what is asked and who is asked is settled in one clause. Capacity is not a concession granted after the fact but the measure by which the demand was framed in the first place, which means the requirement is already fitted to the person before they encounter it. That removes both the excuse that too much is being asked and the anxiety that one is constitutionally unable to answer.

crossReferences.why: Opens with this exact clause and turns it into a prayer not to be burdened beyond endurance.
Attaches the same principle to giving full measure, where perfect accuracy would be impossible.
Applies capacity to spending, and adds that God will bring ease after hardship.

studies.applyIt: Take the religious thing you feel worst about not doing, and ask honestly whether the version in your head was ever sized for your actual life. Then set a version that is. Smaller, and real, and repeatable this month. If it feels disappointingly modest, that is usually the sign that you have finally described something you will still be doing in June.

studies.title: We Would Never Have Found It
studies.meaning: The first thing described is a removal, not an addition. Whatever grudge was in their chests is drawn out, which commentators take as the condition of the place rather than a separate reward. Then the speech, and its structure is careful. Praise for being guided here, followed immediately by the correction that they would never have found the way themselves, and then the acknowledgement that the messengers had told the truth. The answer that comes back attaches the Garden to what they did, using the language of inheritance rather than of payment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The early community was small and made up of people from very different clans, some of whom had long-standing quarrels with each other, and the surah is speaking to an audience for whom inherited grievance was a serious matter. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage is one of the Quran's fullest descriptions of the Garden's inner condition rather than its furnishings, and it comes in a section otherwise given to judgement.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to enter something stealthily, and the same root gives the word for an iron collar. Rancour is pictured as a thing that got inside and then held its owner fast.

keyTerms.gloss: you are made to inherit it
keyTerms.note: The passive of the verb for inheriting. An inheritance is not earned and not bought, which sits deliberately alongside the clause that follows about what they used to do.
Praise given for what someone is as well as for what they have done, unlike thanks, which answers a specific favour. It is the word the Quran opens with, in the same construction as here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feuds in Arabia outlived the men who started them. A killing between two clans could be avenged forty years later by grandsons who had never met the original parties, and poets kept the accounts alive by reciting them at every gathering. Carrying a grievance was not a private failing there; it was an obligation of honour. A place described as having that removed would have sounded, to that audience, like a description of an entirely different kind of society.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran repeatedly describes the Garden as something inherited rather than bought or won, using the same verb in several surahs. Classical commentators harmonise this with the clause about deeds by saying that entry rests on God's mercy while rank within it answers to what a person did, and the two halves of this ayah are the usual evidence cited.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech given to the people of the Garden is a correction of a sentence they have just spoken. They praise God for guiding them here, then add that they would never have been guided otherwise, which withdraws any implication that they found the road. Placing that correction in their own mouths, in the one setting where self-congratulation could do no harm, says something firm about where the tradition locates the origin of guidance.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the removal of rancour from the chest, adding that they face one another as brothers.
Names the inheritors, who will inherit the highest garden and remain in it.
Treats the same problem in this life, calling believers brothers and asking for reconciliation between them.

studies.applyIt: Name one grudge you are still carrying and estimate, honestly, how many hours of your life it has taken. Not whether it is justified; it probably is. Just the hours. Then decide whether you want to keep paying that rate. You do not have to resolve anything today, and you may find the arithmetic does more than a decision would.

studies.title: We Found It True
studies.meaning: The question put across the divide is not a taunt about position. It is about verification. We found what we were promised to be true; did you find yours true. Both groups were told something in advance, and both have now checked it. The answer is a single word, and its bareness is the point. Then an announcer speaks between them, and what he proclaims is not a sentence of punishment but a distancing, since the word for curse in Arabic means being put at a remove from good.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The dispute in Mecca was largely about whether the promise and the warning were real, since the Quraysh treated the resurrection as the least credible part of the message and said so openly. This scene answers by moving to the moment after the question is settled, and by having the confirmation supplied by the people who had denied it rather than by an argument.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making something heard, the same one behind the call to prayer. The Quran uses this exact noun only twice, here and in the Joseph account, both times for a public proclamation.
The root means driving something away and keeping it at a distance. A curse in this vocabulary is exclusion from good rather than a wish for harm, which changes how the proclamation reads.
The neutral verb for a promise, used in the Quran of both the reward and the threat. Its neutrality is what allows the same question to be put to both groups in identical words.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society had no written contracts to fall back on, so a promise was tested only when it came due, and reputations were built entirely on that record. Merchants extended credit on a man's word and found out whether it held a season later. To ask someone whether they found the promise true was to ask the standard question of that economy, and everyone listening knew what the answer settled.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply from the other side is one word in Arabic, and the Quran does not expand it. Classical commentators note the compression: after a lifetime of arguments, objections and demands for proof, the whole position is given up in a syllable, and the narrative moves on immediately without letting anyone comment on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth is presented as something that can be found rather than only argued. The verb both groups use is the verb for coming upon a thing, and it puts the promise and the warning in the same category as facts about the world that eventually declare themselves. This is why the Quran so often addresses disbelief as a matter of patience rather than of proof: the position it takes is that the evidence arrives on its own schedule.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same verifying question at the Fire and receives the same admission, by our Lord, yes.
Gives the answering praise from the other side, that God made His promise to them true.
Records the demand for verification in this life and the instruction to answer that it is certainly true.

studies.applyIt: Think of a promise someone made you that they kept, quietly, at cost to themselves. Tell them you remember it. Most kept promises are never mentioned again by anyone, which is why keeping them is such a good measure of a person. One message today is enough, and it will land harder than you expect.

studies.title: Men Upon The Heights
studies.meaning: The wrongdoers are described first by what they do to others: blocking the road and trying to bend it crooked. Then the scene widens. A partition stands between the two groups, and on the elevated ground above it are men who recognise everyone by their marks. They greet the people of the Garden and have not entered. The last clause is the one commentators dwell on: they are hoping. Who these men are is one of the genuinely open questions of the classical tradition, and the range of answers is wide.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This passage gives the surah its name, and it is among the Quran's most discussed scenes precisely because the text withholds identification. The commentators record several positions: people whose good and bad deeds balanced exactly, or those of high standing placed there to observe, or others. Al-Tabari collects the reports without endorsing one. No occasion of revelation is attached to it.

keyTerms.note: From the root meaning to know or recognise, and used of any raised ridge or crest. The same root supplies the verb in the next clause, so those on the heights are literally on the place of recognising.
A mark placed on something to identify it, used of a brand on livestock and a badge worn in battle. Recognition here is by a visible sign rather than by memory of a face.
A verb for wanting something you have reason to expect but do not yet hold. It sits between confidence and mere wishing, which is why the ayah can end on it without resolving anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Branding was how ownership worked in a herding society. Every tribe had its mark, burned onto camels so that a beast strayed onto other grazing could be identified at a glance from a distance. Battle too was fought with signs worn to tell one side from another in the dust. Recognition by a mark rather than by acquaintance was the ordinary way of knowing who someone belonged to.
studies.didYouKnow: The word that names this surah occurs in only two places in the whole Quran, both within three ayat of each other here. Surah 7 is therefore named after a scene of about four ayat in a chapter of over two hundred, and after a group whose identity the Book deliberately never specifies.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage establishes that the two-sided picture of judgement is not the whole of it. Something stands between, and the people there are not described as suffering. They greet, they observe, and they hope, which introduces a state that is neither settled nor lost. The tradition's refusal to close the question is itself instructive: the Quran gives a place on the map without labelling who occupies it, and the commentators left it that way.

crossReferences.why: Describes a wall raised between two groups, with mercy inside it and punishment on the outer side.
Uses the same idea of recognition by marks, where the guilty are known by their appearance.
Names those genuinely unable to act, whom God may pardon, a category the tradition often reads alongside this.

studies.applyIt: Notice how quickly you sort people into two groups: sound and unsound, ours and theirs, serious and not. This passage introduces a third position and then refuses to define it. Pick one person you have filed under a heading and try holding them unfiled for a week. You do not have to conclude anything. Just leave the folder open.

studies.title: Do Not Place Us There
studies.meaning: The verb is passive. Their eyes are turned towards the other side; nobody says they looked. What follows is a prayer, and its content is worth noticing. They do not ask to be admitted to the Garden and they do not ask for the sight to stop. They ask not to be placed among the wrongdoing people. Commentators read the request as being about company rather than location, since the Arabic names a people rather than a place, and the whole appeal turns on who one ends up standing with.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, within the scene on the heights that gives the surah its name. Its speakers are the men described in the preceding ayah, whose identity the classical tradition never settled. No occasion of revelation is reported. The surah is at this point building its longest continuous piece of dialogue, moving the reader's viewpoint between the two sides and then, here, placing it with people who can see both.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb for diverting something from its direction, used of turning a rider or a stream. The grammar takes the initiative out of their hands, so the sight is something they are shown rather than something they seek.
From the root for meeting or encountering. The word describes direct facing rather than a glance, which is why the ayah reads as a confrontation with a view rather than a passing look.

The ordinary word for a body of people bound together. The plea names a company rather than a punishment, which shifts what is being asked from a place to the question of whose side one is counted on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belonging was survival in Arabia. A man's protection, his marriage prospects and his standing in any dispute followed from the group he was counted with, and expulsion from a tribe was a sentence in itself, whatever the physical conditions. To ask not to be placed among a certain people was, in that world, the most serious request available, and it addressed something more consequential than comfort.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of very few supplications the Quran records as being made after the reckoning has begun, and it asks for something modest. Most prayers reported from that setting are laments or requests to return. Classical commentators note that this one is phrased as a petition still in progress, which is part of why the passage leaves the speakers' outcome open.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer treats company as consequence. What is dreaded is not primarily pain but being counted among a particular people, which suggests that the tradition's picture of the two outcomes is as much about association as about sensation. It also shows a request being made in a place where requests are usually described as closed, which keeps hope operating inside the scene rather than only before it.

crossReferences.why: Asks in this life for the same thing, to be gathered with the righteous rather than among others.
Uses the same construction when facing an overwhelming force, asking for help against a disbelieving people.
Abraham's prayer to be joined to the righteous, which is the positive form of this request.

studies.applyIt: Look at where you spend your unstructured hours and who is in the room, physically or on a screen. Not their character, just the direction they are travelling. You are being shaped by that company whether or not you approve of it. Add one hour this week with someone travelling where you would like to end up, and keep it in the calendar.

studies.title: Your Hoard Did Not Help
studies.meaning: The same men who recognise everyone now address specific figures, and what they name is exactly what those figures had been known for. The word translated as hoardings can mean the wealth a person amassed or the numbers he could muster, and classical commentators take it both ways, since in Arabia the two were nearly the same asset. Alongside it stands the arrogance, named separately. The verb for availing comes from the root for wealth, so the line says, almost literally, that their riches did not make them rich.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The men who led the opposition were the heads of the wealthiest trading houses, and their argument against the message was frequently an argument from position: the leading families had not accepted it, so it could not be sound. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. Placing the challenge in the mouths of onlookers rather than of the vindicated keeps the scene from reading as revenge.

keyTerms.note: The noun covers both a hoard of wealth and a gathered body of men. Commentators read it either way, and in a society where retainers were bought with wealth the ambiguity is not much of a gap.
The verb comes from the root for wealth and independence, so it means to make someone self-sufficient. The sentence therefore uses the vocabulary of riches to say that riches produced nothing.
The same verb the surah applied to the first refusal, in a form meaning to seek greatness for oneself. Its continuous tense makes it a practice rather than an incident.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Mecca was not stored in a vault; it was visible and mobile. It looked like camels, like the number of men who would ride out with you, like the guests at your table during the pilgrimage season. A rich man was rich in the sight of others by definition. This is why the loss described here is total rather than partial: the asset and its display were the same thing.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic here contains a quiet play on words that the English cannot carry. The verb for availing or benefiting is built from the root that gives the words for wealth, riches and self-sufficiency, and one of God's names in the Quran is formed from it. The ayah thus states that their wealth did not enrich them, using one root twice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Property is not condemned in itself here; what is denied is its reach. The passage identifies the specific claim wealth makes, which is that it will be enough, and reports the point at which the claim is tested. Naming arrogance alongside it suggests the tradition sees the two as connected rather than coincidental, since what accumulation most reliably produces is not comfort but the sense of standing above the need for anything else.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing of one man: his wealth and what he earned did not avail him.
Names the day when neither wealth nor sons benefit, except one who comes with a sound heart.
The owner of two gardens argues from being greater in wealth and men, and loses both.

studies.applyIt: Work out what you would still have if the number in your account were halved. List it: skills, relationships, the ability to sleep, whatever is actually on the list. Do it on paper. Most people find the list is longer than they assumed and that almost nothing on it was bought, which is worth knowing before the question is put to you rather than after.

studies.title: Are These The Ones
studies.meaning: A question is put that quotes an old oath back at the people who swore it. They had sworn that God's mercy would never reach a certain group, and that group is now indicated with a gesture. Then, without transition, the words of admission are spoken. Commentators differ over who is addressed by them, whether the people just pointed at or the men on the heights themselves, and the Arabic supports both, which is part of why the passage has been discussed for so long.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The leading families dismissed the early believers precisely by class, objecting that the message had been taken up by slaves, freedmen and the poor, and asking whether God would favour such people over them. That objection is what the oath in this ayah refers to. The Quran answers it not with an argument but by staging the moment when the swearers are shown the outcome.

keyTerms.note: The formal verb for taking an oath, the strongest form of assertion available in Arabic. Quoting it back makes the point that this was not a passing opinion but something they staked their word on.
A verb for obtaining something by reaching out for it, used of picking fruit within arm's length. It makes mercy something that extends towards a person rather than something they climb to.
Grief for something already lost, as distinct from fear, which looks forward. The Quran regularly pairs the two so that both directions of time are covered by a single assurance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a city of ranked families, and the ranking was maintained by public speech. Who could be addressed familiarly, whose son could marry whose daughter, which men's opinions counted in the assembly. Early converts from the weakest layers of that society were an offence to the order itself, and several leading men said openly that they would not sit where such people sat. The oath recalled here belongs to that vocabulary.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran's recurring assurance about fear and grief appears many times, almost always in the third person as a statement about others. Here it is spoken directly to its recipients in the second person, as an address rather than a description, which is a rare form for a phrase that otherwise functions as a formula.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the sharpest limit the Book places on religious judgement of other people. To swear that mercy will not reach someone is to make a claim about a decision that was never anyone's to make, and the scene answers it by simply showing the outcome. It also implies that the error is not merely social snobbery but a theological mistake, since the oath assumes access to information that belongs to God alone.

crossReferences.why: Forbids driving away those who call on their Lord, and names the testing of some people by others.
Tells those who exceeded all bounds not to despair of God's mercy, which covers everything.
Asks whether they are the ones who distribute their Lord's mercy, when God apportions livelihood.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you have privately written off as beyond changing. Say their name and then say, out loud, that you do not know what will happen to them. That is all. You are not obliged to like them or to expect anything. You are giving back a piece of information you were never holding in the first place.

studies.title: Pour Some Water Over Us
studies.meaning: The request is precisely worded. They do not ask for a share; they ask for what overflows, using a verb that means to pour out in abundance, and they name an alternative in case water is not available. The reply is brief and it does not gloat. It states a condition rather than a refusal by the speakers, which commentators note keeps the people of the Garden from being made into the ones withholding. What is described as closed off is not water in general but water for this.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people for whom water was the substance around which the whole society was organised. Mecca itself existed because of a well. The scene follows several ayat of dialogue between the two sides and reverses the direction of the last exchange, since the earlier call went the other way. No occasion of revelation is reported for it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for overflowing, used of a basin brimming over. The same imperative describes the pilgrims surging away from the standing place, so the word carries volume and movement together.
The verb for provision arriving from outside a person's own effort. Its use here concedes the whole argument, since the request acknowledges that what the other side holds came as a gift.
From a root meaning to set apart and make inviolable, the same one behind the words for the sanctuary and for a person under protection. It names a boundary rather than an act of denial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water rights were the hardest currency in Arabia. Wells were owned, guarded and inherited, and a tribe's whole position could rest on one. Refusing water to a traveller was among the deepest disgraces a host could incur, and giving it freely was the standard boast of a generous man. An exchange in which water is asked for and cannot be given would have struck the first listeners as a description of a world with its rules inverted.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used in this request appears in the pilgrimage passages of surah 2 for the movement of the crowds away from the standing place, in the same imperative form. The root describes a liquid overflowing its container and then, by extension, a crowd pouring forward, so the same word covers a brimming basin and a moving multitude.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says something exact about what is lost. It is not that the people of the Fire have nothing, but that the ordinary channels by which one person's abundance reaches another are no longer open. The Quran's picture of this life is full of such channels: hospitality, charity, the well shared with a stranger. Their closure, rather than any described torment, is what this scene chooses to depict.

crossReferences.why: Warns of a day with no trading, no friendship and no intercession, which is the arrangement this scene shows.
Shows a request for light being made across the same divide, and a wall raised between the two groups.
Urges spending before a day comes in which there is no bargaining and no friendship left.

studies.applyIt: Give something away today that costs you almost nothing and that you would normally keep: the last of something, a seat, twenty minutes. Do it without deciding it is significant. The passage is about a moment when the pipes between people are shut, and the only useful response is to keep yours open while they still are.

studies.title: Taken As A Diversion
studies.meaning: Two words are used for what they made of religion, and the Quran elsewhere applies that same pair to worldly life. Here the terms are reversed onto religion itself, so what should have been the serious thing became the entertainment. Then a statement commentators take care over: We forget them as they forgot. Since forgetfulness cannot be attributed to God, they explain it as treating them as one forgotten. The following ayah answers the charge of ignorance in advance. A Book was given, set out in detail, on knowledge.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh response to the recitation was often mockery rather than argument, and several ayat record them talking over it, calling it old tales, and making sport of the warnings. No occasion of revelation is reported. Placing the description of the Book immediately after the charge of frivolity closes the excuse that nothing clear had been provided to be serious about.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be turned aside from what matters. It names amusement by its effect rather than its content, so anything that occupies attention harmlessly can qualify.

keyTerms.gloss: We set it out in detail
keyTerms.note: From the root for a joint between two bones, and for separating things at their natural divisions. A detailed book in this vocabulary is one articulated at its joints rather than one that is merely long.
The classical commentators are agreed that forgetfulness is not attributed to God, and read this as treating them as one forgotten. The wording deliberately mirrors what they did, phrase for phrase.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's entertainment was recitation. Poets held audiences at the seasonal fairs, verses were memorised and repeated, and a striking composition could make a man's name across Arabia. This is exactly the category the opposition tried to put the Quran into, since a poem could be admired, quoted and then set down. Treating something as a performance was a recognised way of neutralising it without ever having to answer it.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words used here for diversion and play appears several times in the Quran, and everywhere else in the Book it describes the life of this world. This is the place where the terms are turned around and applied to religion instead, so the ayah accuses its subjects of exactly reversing which of the two was the serious business.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies a failure that is not disbelief and not hypocrisy. Religion is retained, and it is held lightly, as one of the pleasant furnishings of a life organised around something else. The reply is measured in kind rather than in severity: what was treated as marginal is answered by being treated as absent. And the Book is described as detailed on knowledge, which forecloses the defence that the matter was never made clear enough to take seriously.

crossReferences.why: Instructs leaving those who took their religion as play and diversion, deceived by worldly life.
Applies the same two words to this life itself, which is their usual object in the Quran.
Gives the same reciprocal wording, you forgot Our signs and so today you are forgotten.

studies.applyIt: Look at where religion actually sits in your week: the slot it occupies, the attention it gets compared with the thing you would not miss. Do not judge the answer, just describe it accurately. Then move one thing up a single place in the order, this week only. Not a reform, a reordering, and a small one you will actually complete.

studies.title: Could We Be Sent Back
studies.meaning: The question opens with a word whose root means what a thing comes back to. It is not asking whether they understand the Book but whether they are waiting for its outcome to arrive, which is the only interpretation that will still be available then. Two requests follow, and they are made in the right order and far too late: intercessors first, and failing that, a return in order to act differently. Nothing answers them. The ayah closes in the third person, reporting the loss as already complete.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who maintained figures at the sanctuary precisely on the expectation that they would intercede, and who treated the promised reckoning as a story rather than a date. Both assumptions appear in the two requests here. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage closes the surah's long judgement sequence before it turns to the account of creation and then to the messengers.

keyTerms.gloss: its outcome, what it comes to
keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to return to an origin. The Quran uses the same noun for the interpretation of dreams, so it covers both what a thing means and the event in which the meaning arrives.

From a root meaning to make a thing even by adding a second, as an even number is a pair. An intercessor joins himself to a petitioner so that one becomes two, which is precisely what is missing here.

The passive of the verb for returning something to where it came from, used of goods returned to a seller. The request asks to be handed back, not to go, which concedes that the movement is not theirs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Intercession was the ordinary machinery of Arabian life. A man in trouble did not approach a chief directly; he found someone with standing to speak alongside him, and the whole system of clients and patrons existed to make that possible. Nobody in Mecca thought of intercession as a religious innovation. It was how you got anything done, which is why its absence in this scene is described as the thing that fails.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the arrival of the outcome is the same one that governs the whole Joseph account, where it means the interpretation of a dream that later comes true. In both places the root does double duty: the meaning of a thing and the moment that meaning walks into the room are named by a single word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage distinguishes between recognising the truth and being able to use the recognition. What they say when the outcome arrives is exactly what the messengers had said, word for word, so the content of belief is no longer in dispute at all. What has run out is the time in which believing was an action rather than an observation. That is the Quran's usual account of why the warning is given early and repeated.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same request to be sent back to do righteous work, and the flat refusal that follows.
Shows them wishing to be returned, and states they would return to exactly what they were forbidden.
States the condition intercession operates under: none intercedes with Him except by His permission.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you would do differently if you could go back five years. Now ask what the equivalent thing is today, the one you will name five years from now. It is usually not mysterious. Write it in one sentence and put it where you will see it tomorrow. The passage is about a request that arrives too late; yours has not.

studies.title: His Is The Creation
studies.meaning: After a long stretch of judgement scenes the surah turns and gives its foundation. Creation in six days, then the establishing on the Throne, which the classical commentators affirm as the Quran states it while declining to specify how, some glossing it in terms of sovereignty, all agreeing it implies nothing bodily. Then motion: night pursuing day at speed, the heavenly bodies pressed into service. The summary divides everything in two. His is the making, and His is the ordering, which are not the same claim.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh did not deny a creator; they held that God had made the world and then delegated its running to lesser powers whose favour was worth cultivating. This ayah answers that arrangement precisely, by separating creation from command and assigning both to the same one. No occasion of revelation is reported. It opens the surah's second half, which will be a sequence of messengers all saying the same sentence.

keyTerms.note: The commentators affirm the word as revealed without describing a manner for it, and several explain it in terms of sovereignty assumed. All agree the language rules out anything bodily or spatial.
From a root for urging an animal forward. It turns the succession of night and day into a chase, with one always closing on the other and never quite catching it.
From a root meaning to subject something to work without payment. The sun and moon are described as labourers under orders, which removes them from the category of powers worth appealing to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert life ran on the sky. Travel happened by night to avoid the heat, and direction came from stars that every guide could name; the month began with a sighting of the moon and the whole calendar of markets and pilgrimage followed from it. These were not decorative objects to that audience. They were the instruments by which people found their way and knew what day it was, which is why several of them had attracted worship elsewhere in Arabia.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran states that the heavens and earth were made in six days in seven separate places, always with the same number and never with a breakdown of what happened on each. Classical commentators note that the word rendered as day is used in the Book for stretches of very different length, and they do not assume it means a solar day here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing line does a specific piece of work. Creation and command are separated as two categories and then assigned to one owner, which closes the position that a creator might have withdrawn and left the ordinary running of things to intermediaries. It is a claim about the present tense rather than about origins. And the description of sun, moon and stars as subjected to orders quietly demotes every celestial power the surrounding cultures venerated.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the six days and the Throne, then adds that no one intercedes except after His permission.
Draws the practical conclusion: do not bow to the sun or the moon, but to the one who made them.
Describes the sun unable to overtake the moon and night unable to outrun day, each in an orbit.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight, if you can, and find one thing in the sky you can name. Just one. Stay with it for a minute without reaching for a phone. The people who first heard this ayah navigated by these objects and some of their neighbours worshipped them, and almost nobody now does either. Recovering the first is a decent way to feel the force of the second.

studies.title: Humbly, And In Secret
studies.meaning: Two manners of calling are given rather than two times: lowered, and hidden from other people. A warning about transgressors follows, which the commentators attach to the manner of asking as much as to conduct in general, since the subject here is prayer. The second ayah adds a prohibition against wrecking what has been set right, then returns to prayer with two feelings held together, fear and longing. Mercy is then described as near, and the nearness is given a direction.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah largely concerned with communities that were given a settled land and then ruined it. The prohibition against corrupting the earth after its ordering sits inside that argument, which gives it a historical edge a reader can easily miss. The commentators report no occasion for these two ayat and read them as instruction placed between the accounts of those communities.

keyTerms.note: From a root for lowness and for the udder of an animal, the part that yields when pressed. The word describes a bearing that gives way rather than a feeling, so it can be adopted before it is felt.

Concealment from other people rather than from God. Commentators read it as protecting the request from performance, since a prayer nobody hears cannot be made for anyone's benefit but the one praying.
A strong word, closer to greed than to hope, used of wanting something almost within reach. Paired with fear, it keeps the asking from collapsing into either despair or presumption.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public supplication in Arabia was a performance with an audience. Tribes called on their gods aloud at shrines and before battles, and poets composed the appeals. Rainmaking ceremonies were communal and noisy, and the noise was part of what was thought to work. Telling people to lower their voices and hide the asking removed the social function of prayer entirely.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of fear and eager hope recurs across the Quran as a description of how the righteous pray, and in one passage it describes those who leave their beds at night to call on their Lord. The two words are almost never separated, and classical commentators treat the pair as a single instruction rather than as alternatives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is given a form as well as a content, and both parts of the form work against display. Lowering and hiding remove the two things that turn asking into performance, which is a precise diagnosis of how devotion goes wrong. The closing clause then locates mercy: it is not described as near in general but as near to those who do good, which ties the answer to conduct without making it a transaction.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pair of words for those who call on their Lord at night.
Shows Zachariah calling on his Lord in a hidden voice, the practice described here.
Earlier in the surah, calls for devotion offered sincerely to Him alone.

studies.applyIt: Ask for one thing tonight that you have never said out loud to anyone, in a voice only you can hear. Do not tidy the wording. The ayah asks for two things, lowness and privacy, and the second is easier than people expect once you notice how much of ordinary asking is shaped by an imagined listener.

studies.title: Ahead Of His Mercy
studies.meaning: The winds arrive first, described as carriers of good news sent out in front of the mercy that follows, and the mercy in question is the rain itself, named without a comparison. Then the clouds are lifted, driven to a land that is dead, and water comes down. Fruits of every kind come out. Only after all this does the ayah state its purpose: this is exactly how the dead are brought out. The argument for resurrection is not made from logic but from something the audience watched every year.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Resurrection was the single claim the Quraysh found most absurd, and they returned to it constantly, asking who would revive bones that had crumbled. This passage does not answer with a proof. It points at an annual event that everyone in Arabia depended on and had watched all their lives, and asks them to notice what shape it has. No occasion of revelation is reported.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected to the skin, since news of this kind shows on a face before it is spoken. The winds are cast as messengers running ahead rather than as weather.
From a root meaning to be small or light. The verb means to find something light enough to pick up, so heavy clouds are described as an easy load for the wind that carries them.
The ordinary verb for driving livestock to pasture or to water. Clouds are herded, which continues the picture of the whole system as animals moving under a driver's hand.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rain in Arabia was an event, not a season. A wadi that had been bare stone for a year would carry water within hours, and grazing appeared where nothing had grown. Whole tribes moved on the report of it, and scouts were sent to watch for cloud on the horizon. Nobody in that audience needed to be told what a dead land looked like or what happened to it three days after water arrived.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah changes speaker in the middle. It begins with He sends the winds, in the third person, and then shifts to We drove them, We sent down, We brought out, before returning to the third person at the close. This turning is a recognised feature of the Quran's style, and here it places the divine voice directly inside the sequence at the moment the water falls.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is presented as a familiar process rather than an unprecedented one. The passage does not argue that God is able to do it; it argues that He is visibly doing it, on a schedule, in front of people who have stopped registering what they are watching. Calling rain mercy without a comparison makes the same move in the other direction, treating an ordinary physical event as a direct instance of a divine attribute rather than an illustration of one.

crossReferences.why: Points at the traces of God's mercy reviving the earth and draws the identical conclusion about the dead.
Gives almost the same sequence, winds stirring clouds driven to a dead land, ending on the resurrection.
Calls the water blessed, lists what grows from it, and names it as the coming out.

studies.applyIt: Find something growing near you that you did not plant: a weed in a pavement crack, a tree on your street, moss on a wall. Stand near it for thirty seconds and work out where its water came from. The passage rests entirely on people noticing a process they were already living inside, and this is the smallest available version of that.

studies.title: The Good Land And The Bad
studies.meaning: Two plots of ground receive the same rain and return different things. The good land yields its growth; the poor land gives up almost nothing, and the word for what it produces means grudging and meagre at once. The classical commentators read the two grounds as a likeness for two hearers of the same revelation, since the ayah follows directly on the rain that was just described as the pattern of resurrection. The closing clause names who benefits from signs being turned about in different forms, and the qualification is thankfulness.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the run of ayat that use the natural world to answer objections about resurrection. Arabia had both kinds of ground within a day's ride: fertile pockets around springs and oases, and salt flats and stony ground where the same downpour produced a few bitter shoots. The comparison needed no explaining. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: A word for what is pleasant, clean and fit for use, applied in the Quran to food, speech, dwellings and land. It names suitability for purpose rather than moral goodness in the abstract.
A rare word describing something given up unwillingly and in small quantity. The Quran uses it nowhere else, and it carries both the poverty of the yield and the reluctance of the giving.
From a root for turning a thing this way and that, used of changing the winds' direction and of exchanging currency. The signs are described as presented from different angles rather than repeated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A farmer at an oasis knew his ground plot by plot and could tell you which corner would repay the water and which would not. Palm cultivation depended on that knowledge, and land was valued by it. Salt ground looked identical to good ground after a rain, and the difference showed only weeks later at harvest. The comparison here therefore describes something slow and only visible in the yield.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for varying the signs recurs across the Meccan surahs, and each time it is attached to a different audience: people who are thankful here, people who understand elsewhere, people who know. Classical commentators treat the changing endings as significant. The same material is being presented repeatedly, and the Quran keeps naming a different quality that lets it land.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Receptivity is located in the receiver rather than in the message. The rain is the same rain, and the difference in outcome is entirely a property of the ground, which puts the responsibility for hearing where the passage has already been putting it. Naming thankfulness as the qualifying condition is unexpected, since one might expect intelligence or sincerity, and it suggests that what prepares a person for revelation is the habit of noticing what has been given.

crossReferences.why: Uses a matching likeness of water in valleys and metal in fire, separating what stays from what is carried off.
Sets a good word as a rooted tree against a corrupt word as a shrub torn from the surface.
Describes rain falling on a rock with soil on it, washing it bare, as a likeness for spoiled giving.

studies.applyIt: Think of a piece of good advice you were given twice, once when it bounced off and once when it landed. Nothing about the advice changed. Work out what was different about you on the second occasion. Whatever that was, it is the thing worth protecting, and most people find it had something to do with what they had recently been grateful for.

studies.title: I Fear For You
studies.meaning: The surah begins its sequence of messengers here, and the first speech sets the pattern all the others will follow. The address is intimate: my people, spoken by a man to his own community. The instruction is one clause, and the reason is one clause. Then a sentence that is easy to misread. The Arabic preposition makes it fear on their behalf rather than fear of them, so what is stated is not a threat delivered but an anxiety carried, which is a very different posture for a warner to occupy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Every messenger in this stretch of the surah speaks to his own people, and the parallel with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) addressing the Quraysh is left for the reader to draw rather than stated. The Quran gives the flood tradition without the surrounding detail found in older scriptures. No occasion of revelation is reported. The sequence runs from the earliest of these communities forward, ending with one the audience could still visit.

keyTerms.note: The possessive ending is doing the work. He does not say O people but claims them as his own, which places him inside the community he is warning rather than opposite it.
From a root whose related words include a path worn smooth by walking. Worship in this vocabulary is a settled course of life rather than a set of occasions.

The preposition turns the fear outward onto them. A warner who says he fears for his audience is describing his own distress, not issuing a threat, and the wording is preserved in every parallel telling.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The men who spoke for a tribe were its elders and its poets, and their authority came from being of the blood. An outsider bringing a warning could be ignored; a man of your own clan telling you the arrangement you all lived by was wrong was a far more disturbing thing, because he had nothing to gain and everything to lose. That is the position every messenger in this surah occupies, and it was the Prophet's position in Mecca.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact sentence, worship God, you have no god other than Him, is spoken by four different messengers in this surah in almost identical Arabic: here, and then by the messengers to three later communities. The Quran presents them as delivering one message rather than founding four religions, and it makes the point through repetition rather than by asserting it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is defined here by content rather than by biography. What makes a messenger is the sentence he says, and that sentence is shown to be the same across enormous stretches of time and completely unrelated peoples. The warning that follows is presented as care rather than coercion, which sets the tone for the whole sequence: each of these men will be refused, and none of them is described as having wanted the confrontation.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same mission at length in a surah devoted to it, with the call described night and day.
Repeats this sentence word for word, showing how fixed the formula is across the Quran.
The parallel opening, where he calls himself a clear warner to his people in the same terms.

studies.applyIt: Think of a warning you once gave someone that came out as an accusation. Most do. The difference is usually one preposition: I am worried about you rather than you are doing this wrong. If there is someone you need to say something to this week, try building the sentence around your own worry instead of their fault, and notice how differently it is received.

studies.title: I Know What You Do Not
studies.meaning: The objection comes from the notables, and it is a diagnosis rather than an argument: we see you in obvious error. The reply is remarkable for what it does not do. It offers no counter-accusation and no proof. It denies the charge in a single clause, states a position, and then gives three activities in order: I deliver, I counsel sincerely, and I know from God what you do not know. Commentators note that the last is the only claim of superiority made in the whole exchange, and it is a claim about a source rather than about a person.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The word for the notables describes the men who filled an assembly and whose opinion settled matters, and it recurs throughout this surah as the standing source of opposition. That was the Quraysh arrangement too, where a handful of clan heads spoke for the city. No occasion of revelation is reported. The Quran presents the same social pattern across every community in the sequence without commenting on the repetition.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to fill. They are the men who fill a gathering, whose presence makes it official. The word is social rather than legal, describing weight of standing rather than any formal office.

They charged him with straying using one form of the word; he answers with a different form that names a single occurrence. Commentators read the switch as denying even the smallest instance rather than only the general charge.
From a root meaning pure and unmixed, used of honey without wax. Counsel of this kind has nothing of the counsellor's own interest folded into it, which is the whole of his defence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribal assembly met in the open and decided by weight rather than by vote. A few men spoke, the rest listened, and a proposal that the leading voices dismissed was finished. Speaking against that consensus meant standing alone in front of everyone you knew, with no procedure to appeal to. The scene here is not a debate between equals. It is one man answering the room that decides what the community believes.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply reverses the sentence structure of the accusation rather than contradicting its content. They said we see you in straying; he says there is no straying in me, moving the word from a place he occupies to a thing that might be inside him, and denying it there. The Arabic makes the shift visible in a way English translation cannot easily carry.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Claimed knowledge is grounded in transmission rather than in insight. The messenger does not say he is wiser or that he reasoned his way to something; he says he knows from God, which makes his authority entirely dependent and therefore checkable against the message rather than against his person. That distinction runs through the Quran's whole account of prophecy and is why messengers are shown correcting themselves and being corrected.

crossReferences.why: Has him disclaim knowledge of the unseen, treasuries and angelic status, limiting the claim precisely.
Gives the same confrontation, where the objection is that the lowest people follow him.
Puts the identical limitation in the Prophet's mouth: he follows only what is revealed to him.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you are told you are simply wrong, with no reason attached. The instinct is to argue or to fold. There is a third option here: deny the charge once, plainly, say what you are actually claiming, and stop. It takes about fifteen seconds and it ends more conversations well than either of the alternatives.

studies.title: A Man From Among You
studies.meaning: The question turns the objection into the evidence. They found it strange that the reminder came through an ordinary man of their own community; the ayah asks why that should be surprising rather than expected. Three purposes are then given in a rising order: to warn, so that you may guard yourselves, and so that you may be shown mercy. The sequence moves from an unpleasant beginning to a merciful end, which reframes the warning itself as the first step of a favour rather than as the point.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quraysh objection to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was in exactly this shape. They knew him, his family and his circumstances, and the familiarity was the problem: a message of that weight ought to have arrived by way of an angel or at least a great man of one of the two cities. Putting the same objection in the mouth of a far older community lets the answer be given without argument.

keyTerms.note: From a root for wonder and astonishment. The question is not rhetorical padding; it asks them to examine their own surprise, on the assumption that the surprise itself is the thing worth explaining.

Indefinite, so a reminder rather than the reminder. Calling revelation a reminder assumes the content is already partly known and that the failure being addressed is inattention rather than ignorance.
Both words matter. He is a man, not another order of being, and he is from you, so his life and lineage are known and his conduct can be checked against what he says.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Familiarity was the difficulty. In a city of a few thousand, everyone knew who had been a boy running errands twenty years earlier, whose uncle had failed in trade, who had married into which clan. Nothing about a man was hidden, and prophethood conferred no new appearance or voice. The people being addressed had watched the messenger grow up, and that was precisely the evidence they used against him.
