studies.didYouKnow: This question appears twice in this surah in nearly identical words, once here and once a few ayat later addressed to a different people entirely. The Quran does not remark on the repetition. It simply lets the same sentence be spoken to two communities separated by an enormous span of time, and leaves the reader to notice that the objection had not changed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ordinariness of the messenger is defended as a feature rather than excused as a limitation. A message delivered by a being of another order could be admired without being followed, since nothing about that life would be reproducible. The passage also arranges its three purposes so that mercy is the destination and warning is only the road, which sets a frame for every threatening passage in the surah around it.

crossReferences.why: Reports the identical astonishment that revelation came to a man from among them, and calls it plain sorcery.
Records the objection in its social form: why was this not sent to a great man of the two towns.
Answers the objection directly, saying an angel messenger would have suited angels, not people.

studies.applyIt: Think of something true you dismissed because of who said it: a relative you find tiresome, a colleague you had already filed away. Go back to the content once, in your head, with the speaker removed. If it still holds, act on it this week without telling them where you got it. The point is not to give credit. It is to stop losing information.

studies.title: A People Without Sight
studies.meaning: The entire flood is given in a single ayah. There is no ark-building, no mockery from the shore, no waters bursting from the earth, no bird sent out. Three verbs carry it: they denied, We rescued, We drowned. Then the closing judgement, which is not about wrongdoing but about perception. They were a blind people. Commentators uniformly take this as blindness of the heart rather than of the eyes, since the whole preceding exchange has been about men who looked at a messenger and saw an error.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Surah 11 and surah 71 give this account at length, with the building of the ship, the exchanges with the community, and the loss of a son. Here the compression is deliberate, because the surah is running six of these narratives in sequence and the shape they share is the subject rather than any one of them. No occasion of revelation is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: An unusual noun that takes the same form whether one vessel or many is meant. The Quran uses it for a single ark here and for whole fleets elsewhere without changing a letter.
From a root meaning to bring something out to high ground away from danger. Rescue in this word is removal to safety rather than defence in place, which fits a flood exactly.

The plural of the ordinary word for a blind person. The commentators read it here of the heart, and the Quran elsewhere states directly that it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had ships. Coastal traders sailed the Red Sea, and Meccan merchants knew vessels from the ports at Jeddah and Shu'ayba, but the interior had nothing of the sort and water arrived only as flash flood in a dry valley. A rescue by ship was therefore a foreign and slightly exotic picture to an inland audience, while drowning in a wadi that filled without warning was something whole caravans had died of.
studies.didYouKnow: The flood occupies one ayah here and most of a surah elsewhere. Surah 71 is named after this messenger and gives his complaint in his own words across twenty-eight ayat, while surah 11 supplies the ark and the son. Reading them together shows the Quran deliberately telling one story at several lengths depending on what each surah is doing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denial is diagnosed as an incapacity rather than a conclusion. The community is not called stubborn or wicked in this summary; it is called blind, which locates the failure in what they could take in rather than in what they decided. The Quran uses this diagnosis carefully. It appears at the end of long exchanges, after the arguments have been given and refused, and it explains why more argument would not have helped.

crossReferences.why: States the principle behind this verdict: eyes do not go blind, hearts within the chests do.
Gives the account this ayah compresses, including the ship, the waves and the son who refused.
Tells the same events in short rhythmic lines and calls the ark a sign left behind.

studies.applyIt: Ask someone close to you what they can see about your situation that you cannot. Then do not explain, defend, or supply the context they are missing. Just write it down. Blindness of this kind is defined by not being visible from inside, which means the only way to check for it is to borrow someone else's eyes for five minutes.

studies.title: And To Aad, Their Brother
studies.meaning: The second messenger arrives with almost no preamble. He is introduced as their brother, which the commentators take as kinship of descent rather than of belief, since he came from among the people he addressed. His opening sentence is word for word the one just spoken by the messenger before him. Only the closing clause differs, and it is a question rather than a statement of fear. The construction of the ayah itself makes the argument: two different peoples, separated by generations, receiving one message.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were an Arabian people, placed by the Quran in the sand dunes of the south, and their ruins and reputation were part of the audience's own inherited history rather than a foreign tradition. Along with Thamud they belong to the Arabs' account of themselves. Putting them in a sequence beside the flood generation was a claim that local history and universal history are the same history.

keyTerms.note: Used across this sequence for each messenger. The commentators read it as brotherhood of lineage, since each man was of the people he was sent to, which is what made ignoring him difficult.

An ancient Arabian people the Quran associates with the sand tracts of the south. Their name entered proverb: something very old was said to be from the time of Aad long before this surah was recited.

A question built from the verb meaning to place a shield between yourself and harm. Asking rather than commanding leaves the audience to supply the answer, which is why the sequence uses it repeatedly.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Aad were proverbial in Arabia the way ancient empires are proverbial elsewhere. Poets invoked them for antiquity, and the phrase from the days of Aad meant impossibly long ago. Southern Arabia held visible remains of substantial civilisations, and the incense route ran past them. When this surah names them, it is not introducing an unfamiliar people. It is picking up a name the audience already used in ordinary speech.
studies.didYouKnow: Aad and Thamud are the two peoples in this sequence with no parallel in the older scriptures, and both are Arabian. The Quran sets them among the flood generation and the communities of Lot and Midian without marking any difference in status, which places the audience's own regional past inside the same account as the traditions they had heard from their Jewish and Christian neighbours.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The repetition of the identical opening sentence is itself a theological claim. If every messenger says the same thing, then the differences between religious communities are not differences in what was sent, and each community's tradition is a version of one message rather than a rival to the others. The word brother matters for the same reason: revelation arrives inside a people, in their own language and lineage, rather than being imported.

crossReferences.why: Places this messenger and his people among the sand dunes, and repeats the warning he gave them.
The parallel introduction in surah 11, with the same brother formula and the same opening sentence.
Describes what became of them and names the boast that preceded it, who is greater in strength.

studies.applyIt: Learn one thing this week about a religious tradition near you that you know almost nothing about, from a source inside it rather than a summary written by an outsider. Not to agree with it. The passage insists that messengers came to every people in their own idiom, and finding out what someone actually holds is the smallest form of taking that seriously.

studies.title: A Trustworthy Adviser
studies.meaning: The charge escalates from the one made to the messenger before him. That one was called mistaken; this one is called light-minded and, in a second clause, suspected of lying. The reply follows the same pattern as before, denying the charge in one clause without returning the insult. What is new is the ending. He does not say he knows what they do not; he offers a description of himself as an adviser who can be relied on, which is a claim about character that the audience was in a position to check.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The word he uses of himself was, in that city, a title rather than an adjective: the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been known as the trustworthy one before revelation began, and his reputation for it had been established in disputes the Quraysh themselves brought to him. Putting the same word in an ancient messenger's mouth let the audience hear their own knowledge of a man's record as a form of evidence.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning lightness and flimsiness, used of thin cloth and a slack rope. It accuses him not of being wrong but of being insubstantial, which is a harder charge to answer than an error.

The verb covers supposition, suspicion and confident opinion. They are not claiming proof, and the wording concedes as much, which is why the accusation and the emphatic particle attached sit oddly together.
From the root behind the words for faith, security and safety. Someone described this way is one with whom things can be deposited, and the word was used in Arabia of a man who held goods for others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Commerce in Mecca ran on deposits. Merchants left goods and money with men they trusted while they travelled, with no paper and no court to enforce anything, so a reputation for holding what was not yours was the most valuable asset a man could own. It took years to build and one incident to destroy. To call yourself reliable in that setting was to invite the whole city to check.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this messenger uses of himself is the same one the people of Mecca had used of the Prophet for years before the first revelation, so long that it functioned as his name in disputes. The Quran does not point this out. It simply has an ancient messenger use the word, in front of an audience that had used it themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two kinds of credential are set beside each other across these exchanges. One messenger appeals to knowledge from God, which cannot be checked from outside; this one appeals to a record of conduct, which can. The Quran presents both as legitimate and neither as sufficient alone. The pairing suggests that a message is authenticated by the life carrying it as much as by its source, which is why the sequence keeps describing what these men were like.

crossReferences.why: Has the earlier messenger describe himself in exactly these words, a trustworthy messenger to his people.
The king describes Joseph with the same word after testing him, establishing it as a public verdict.
Applies the same word to the angel bringing the revelation, obeyed there and trustworthy.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing someone has left in your keeping: money, a confidence, a task nobody is checking on. Do the reliable thing with it this week before anyone asks. Trustworthiness is not a feeling and it is not a claim; it is a record that accumulates quietly and is only ever noticed in its absence.

studies.title: Remember The Favours
studies.meaning: The same question is asked as before, then the argument changes direction entirely. Instead of pressing the warning, he tells them to remember two things: that they were made successors after the earlier community, and that they were given an increase in build. Commentators read that increase as physical stature, as strength, or as scope and abundance generally, and the word is broad enough for all three. Then a general instruction to recall God's favours, with prosperity as the stated outcome rather than escape from punishment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Aad were remembered in Arabia for size and power, and their own boast, recorded elsewhere in the Quran, was that nobody was stronger than they were. The argument here takes that boast and returns it to them as a gift received rather than a quality possessed. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage sits between the objection and the refusal, as the last attempt made before the exchange breaks down.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow behind and to take another's place. Being a successor implies a predecessor who is gone, so the word contains a warning inside a compliment.
From a verb for spreading a thing out and opening the hand. Commentators read it of bodily size, of strength, or of abundance and reach, and the word does not force a choice.
An unusual plural for good things given. It is the word repeated as a refrain throughout one whole surah, asking which of the Lord's favours the hearers would deny.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Succession was how Arabs understood the map. A tribe held a territory because another had held it before and had gone, driven out, absorbed or destroyed, and every well and grazing ground had that history attached. Nobody thought of their land as originally theirs. To be reminded that you are the successors of a vanished people was to be reminded of something you already recited in your own genealogy.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for favours is rare, and it is the one repeated as the refrain of surah 55, where a single question about the Lord's bounties is put thirty-one times. Its appearance in this speech connects a warning delivered to an ancient Arabian people with the Quran's most sustained catalogue of what has been given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is offered as an argument rather than as a duty, and it is put to people who are refusing a warning. The reasoning is that a community which correctly identifies where its strength came from will not mistake the strength for a guarantee. This is why the passage names the vanished predecessors in the same breath as the gift: the two facts belong together, and holding only one of them is what produces the confidence being addressed.

crossReferences.why: Records their boast, who is greater than us in strength, which this ayah answers in advance.
The refrain built on the same rare word, asking which of the Lord's favours would be denied.
Names humanity as successors on the earth, raised in ranks, and calls the arrangement a test.

studies.applyIt: Write down three things about your circumstances that you did not arrange: where you were born, a body that works, someone who taught you to read. Then note who held that same advantage before you and no longer does. The passage puts the gift and the predecessor in one sentence, and it is the pairing rather than either half that does the work.

studies.title: God Alone, And Abandon
studies.meaning: The objection is precise and it is worth reading slowly. They do not refuse to worship God. They refuse the word alone, and they name the cost attached to it, which is leaving what their fathers served. Commentators point out that this is the actual point of friction in every one of these narratives: not the existence of God but His exclusivity, since exclusivity requires abandoning something. Then the demand, which changes the subject from argument to spectacle. Bring the thing you threaten, if you are telling the truth.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the objection is a transcript of the Quraysh position. Mecca acknowledged a supreme God and maintained many lesser figures at the sanctuary, whose upkeep was tied to the city's standing and income. What the message asked for was not belief in a creator, which they already had, but the removal of everything else, which touched livelihood and lineage together. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A single word carrying the whole dispute. Their complaint attaches to it rather than to the name of God, which is why the Quran's argument with them is so often about exclusivity rather than existence.
An old verb the language uses in only some of its forms. It means to let something go and walk away from it, which names the actual expense of the demand being refused.
The neutral verb for a promise, used here of a threatened outcome. Its neutrality lets the sentence be read as a dare, since they are demanding delivery of something offered as a warning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tribe's gods were inherited property, kept in a household or at a shrine and tied to specific places, seasons and rights. Abandoning them was not a change of opinion; it was walking away from an inheritance, breaking with the men who had held it before you, and telling your relatives that they had spent their lives on nothing. The social cost of the word alone was the whole difficulty, and everyone in this exchange understood it.
studies.didYouKnow: The demand at the end of this ayah, bring us what you promise if you are truthful, reappears almost word for word later in this same surah from a different community entirely. The Quran gives the identical challenge to two peoples with nothing else in common, which is one of the ways the sequence makes the pattern visible without stating it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates disbelief in cost rather than in doubt. These people accept the argument and refuse the consequence, which is a different condition from being unconvinced and is treated as more serious. Demanding the punishment as proof completes the picture: they are willing to have the question settled by an event they cannot survive, but not by a change they would have to make while alive.

crossReferences.why: Describes their chests shrinking when God alone is mentioned, and lifting at the mention of others.
Records the Quraysh saying the same thing, that making the gods one god is an astonishing demand.
Gives the same dare in Mecca: send down stones from the sky if this is the truth from You.

studies.applyIt: Identify one thing you would have to give up if you took your own convictions completely seriously. Not a vice, necessarily; more likely a habit, a comfort, or an arrangement that suits you. You do not have to give it up today. Just stop pretending the reluctance is an intellectual difficulty. Naming it accurately as a cost is the honest first move.

studies.title: Names You Yourselves Gave
studies.meaning: The reply opens by stating that something has already fallen on them, using a word whose classical range runs from defilement to punishment to divine anger, and the commentators record the spread without settling it. Then the sharpest sentence in the sequence. Are you disputing with me about names, which you and your fathers named, for which God sent down no warrant. The argument is not that the objects of worship are weak. It is that they are words, given by people, and that nothing beyond the naming was ever added.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the argument transfers exactly to the Quraysh. The figures at the sanctuary had names, genealogies and stories, all of local manufacture, and the Quran repeatedly presses the question of who authorised any of it. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The closing line, wait and I am waiting with you, ends the exchange without a further appeal, which is how several of these confrontations in the surah close.

keyTerms.note: The commentators differ over its sense here, reading it as filth, as punishment, or as divine displeasure. All the readings agree that something has already settled on them rather than being merely threatened.
Indefinite and plural, so mere names. The argument reduces the objects of the dispute to labels, and then observes that the labelling was done entirely by the people now defending them.
In the Quran this word usually means the proof that licenses a claim rather than political power. Nothing was sent down to back the names, so the whole structure rests on assertion.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Naming was a serious act in Arabia. A poet could fix a nickname on a man that his descendants carried for centuries, and tribes took their identity from an ancestor's name and defended it. Words were understood to make things real in a way that a written culture finds harder to feel. This is why the reduction of the gods to names is such a pointed argument, and why it would have stung rather than seemed obvious.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact argument appears in three widely separated places in the Quran, always in the same form: they are only names which you and your fathers named, with no warrant sent down for them. One instance is spoken by an ancient messenger here, one by Joseph in a prison, and one about three specific figures venerated in Arabia.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a test to religious language itself. A name can be inherited, defended and fought over while nothing behind it was ever established, and the Quran treats the gap between the word and the warrant as the thing to examine. It is an argument that cuts inward as much as outward, since any tradition can accumulate terms that carry weight because they are old rather than because anything was sent down about them.

crossReferences.why: Joseph makes the identical argument to his cellmates, that they serve only names their fathers gave.
Applies the same sentence to three figures venerated in Arabia, following conjecture and desire.
Notes that they serve what God sent down no warrant for, and of which they have no knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Pick a word you use in religious conversation that you have never actually defined for yourself. Everyone has several. Write down what you mean by it in one sentence, without borrowing a phrase. If you cannot, that is worth knowing, and the fix is a question to someone who can, not an argument with anyone who uses it differently.

studies.title: Call Him By His Names
studies.meaning: Two statements with an instruction between them. The names belong to God, they are described as the most beautiful, and the response asked for is to use them in calling on Him. The commentators note that the ayah neither lists them nor fixes their number. Then a second instruction, to leave alone those who distort the names, which is unusually restrained: no argument is prescribed, only withdrawal, with the outcome left where it belongs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators connect the ayah with the practice of deriving names for local deities from the divine name itself, which is what the word for distortion is taken to describe. The surah has spent much of its length on invented religion, and this ayah addresses the same problem at the level of vocabulary rather than at the level of ritual.

keyTerms.note: A superlative in the feminine, from a root for beauty and for what is good. It qualifies the names as a set, so the beauty is claimed for the whole vocabulary rather than for any single term in it.
The verb covers both calling someone by a name and calling on them for help. The ayah uses both senses at once, so naming and asking become a single action rather than two separate ones.
From a root for turning aside, related to the word for a grave niche cut off to one side. It describes bending a name away from its proper direction rather than denying it outright.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names carried power in Arabia. A person's name announced lineage and often obligation, oaths were sworn by names, and poets attacked enemies by twisting theirs. Deities were addressed with strings of titles, and knowing the right form of address was thought to affect whether an appeal was heard. Instruction about which names to use was practical religious advice, not a matter of style.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran never gives a closed list of these names. The phrase occurs four times, always in the same form, and the familiar lists compiled later were drawn from across the whole text by scholars rather than presented anywhere as a single passage. The number most often cited comes from a report rather than from the Quran itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowledge of God is presented as vocabulary given for use, not as information to be held. The instruction is to call, which makes the names instruments of relationship rather than items of doctrine. And the handling of opponents is notably light: distortion is named as a real fault and then left alone, with no correction demanded, placing the matter between them and God rather than in a dispute to be won.

crossReferences.why: Runs a long sequence of the names, closing with the same phrase used here.
Says either name may be used in calling, since the beautiful names belong to Him.
States the same phrase as a single sentence about the one worthy of worship.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the divine names you rarely think about and use it once a day this week when you ask for something, choosing it to fit what you are actually asking for. The ayah joins naming to asking. Most people default to two or three names, and the difference a different one makes is worth noticing.

studies.title: Take What Comes Easily
studies.meaning: Three instructions arrive in one line, and the first is the most discussed. The word can mean pardon or what is surplus and easily given, so the commentators read it as accepting what people readily offer rather than pressing them, and also as forgiving. A warning about provocation follows, with a practical response: take refuge. Then a description of the God-conscious, who remember and then see, set against those who are dragged on without stopping.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the end of a long surah that has run through the destruction of earlier communities and the arguments of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) with his own people. These closing instructions are addressed to him about how to conduct that argument. The commentators record several reports about the first ayah, all of them turning on how a person deals with those who will not listen.

keyTerms.note: The root covers both forgiving and surplus. Commentators take it here as accepting what people offer without pressing them to their limit, which is why the same word can also mean pardon.
Not the uninformed. The word names people who act without restraint, and older poetry uses it for hot-headedness, so avoiding them means declining a fight rather than avoiding the uneducated.
A sudden jab, the word used of driving an animal forward with a point. It names the suggestion as brief and external rather than as a settled state, which is why the response given is immediate.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab honour culture required an answer to every provocation, and skilled opponents provoked deliberately, knowing that an angry man could be manoeuvred into a costly quarrel. Poets baited each other in public for exactly that reason. Turning away read as weakness. The instruction to decline the exchange was not passive advice in that setting; it cut against the main mechanism of social standing.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to take refuge is followed two ayat later by an account of what taking refuge looks like from the inside: a person remembers, and then sees. The classical commentators follow that sequence closely, since the passage moves from an external command to an internal description of it working, which is unusual in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats provocation as something that happens to a person rather than as something they are. That distinction does a great deal of work: the sudden impulse is described as a jab from outside, and the response asked for is not suppression but relocation, taking shelter somewhere. And the contrast at the end is not between good people and bad, but between those who notice and those who are pulled along without ever stopping.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction with a reason, repelling harm with what is better.
Describes the servants of the Merciful answering the ignorant with peace.
Preserves a supplication for refuge from the promptings of devils.

studies.applyIt: The next time you feel the sharp pull to answer something, name it as a jab rather than as your own opinion, and wait until you have finished one slow breath. The passage puts a specific move in that gap. It does not say the provocation was unreal; it says the response is a place you go rather than a thing you win.

studies.title: Listen, And Be Silent
studies.meaning: A demand is reported and refused. When no sign is produced, the opponents suggest he should simply have devised one, and the reply concedes nothing about his own resources: he follows what is revealed, and does not compose. The text then names itself as insight, guidance and mercy. The second ayah turns to the listener with two instructions, hearing and silence, and attaches an outcome to them that is left as a hope rather than a promise.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah. The demand for a produced sign runs through the whole Meccan period. The commentators connect the second ayah with how people behaved during recitation, though the reports vary: some link it to the prayer, others to any occasion of hearing. What the two ayat share is a shift from arguing about the Quran to describing how it is to be received.

keyTerms.note: A verb for picking something out and gathering it for yourself. The taunt assumes composition, so the choice of word makes the accusation precise: they are asking him to produce, not to transmit.
The plural of a word for inner sight, formed like an instrument. It names the text as something you see by rather than something you look at, which is why the ayah pairs it with guidance.
A verb specifically for stopping your own speech in order to hear. It is added after the command to listen, so attention and silence are named separately and each is asked for on its own.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was heard, not read, and audiences at the fairs listened with a critical ear and interrupted freely. Recitation was public and competitive, and a listener's noise was itself a form of judgement. Reports describe opponents at Mecca urging one another to drown out the recitation with talk and clamour. Telling listeners to fall silent addressed a real tactic, not merely a matter of manners.
studies.didYouKnow: This is among the places in the Quran where the text describes the correct behaviour towards itself. The surah ends two ayat later with a prostration, one of the passages at which readers traditionally prostrate during recitation, so the instruction to listen is immediately followed by an instruction the body carries out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to produce a sign on demand defines prophecy negatively: the messenger's role excludes invention, and admitting that publicly costs him the argument in the short term. The passage then relocates the evidence into the text itself, calling it insight rather than proof. And the instruction to listen implies that something is transmitted in the hearing which cannot be obtained by discussing it afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Records the same demand to alter the Quran and the same refusal to change it.
Lists the specific signs demanded of him and the answer given to them.
Describes what happens to believers when the ayat are recited to them.

studies.applyIt: The next time you hear the Quran recited, whether you follow the words or not, stop what you are doing for the length of one passage and give it nothing but attention. No phone, no half-listening. The ayah asks for two separate things, hearing and silence, and most of us have got out of the habit of the second.
